question: How can someone demonstrate that bitcoins were destroyed forever rather than just moved to a wallet they control?
rubric: Mentions OP_RETURN outputs as provably unspendable by consensus
Mentions scripts that always resolve to false
Mentions addresses derived from a hash with no feasible pre-image (e.g. all-zero hash)
Distinguishes 'eater' vanity addresses as only probabilistically unspendable
Penalize: suggesting simply deleting your own private key proves a burn

in_pack_facts.quote: Put the coins in an `OP_RETURN` output. These outputs are provably unspendable because the consensus rules prevent it.
Note that this address isn't provably unspendable, it is just super duper unlikely that someone knows the private key for it.

source.title: How does one prove that they sent bitcoins to an unspendable wallet? Proof of burn?

question: My university won't give me a fixed IP for a Bitcoin full node. Will a changing address hurt the node?
rubric: States a dynamic IP works fine for a full node
Mentions dynamic DNS if a name pointer is needed
Explains static IP helps inbound connections because peers remember addresses
States outbound connections, the important ones, are unaffected
Penalize: claiming a static IP is required to sync or validate the chain

in_pack_facts.quote: Static IP has no effect on your outbound connections (which, to your node, are the most important, not the inbound ones).
It would simply require some additional work to set up a dynamic dns service

source.title: Set up a Bitcoin full node: static or dynamic IP address?

question: Explain what sets bitcoin's dollar price when no central bank issues or backs it.
rubric: States price is set by supply and demand / perception rather than an issuer
Draws the comparison with fiat money valued by trust
Mentions news, adoption and incidents (hacks, outages) shifting demand
Mentions speculation dominates over transactional demand
Penalize: claiming a central authority or the developers set the price

in_pack_facts.quote: Bitcoin follows the same principle, in that its value is determined by perception.
With most of the value of bitcoin currently attributed to speculation

source.title: What determines a bitcoin's value?

question: Describe what happens to a bitcoin transaction between broadcasting it and its inclusion in a block.
rubric: Says nodes validate the transaction on receipt and drop invalid ones
Mentions the mempool and relaying to peers
Mentions miners pick transactions (higher fees more likely) and blocks come about every 10 minutes
Explains confidence grows with each subsequent block (confirmations)
Penalize: saying the transaction is only validated when the block is mined

in_pack_facts.quote: If it is not valid, it will be discarded, but if it is valid it will be added to that node's mempool.
is "mined" every 10 minutes on average

source.title: How long a high-priority transaction takes to evaluate

question: If I just leave the Bitcoin Core wallet running on my PC, will it slowly earn me coins?
rubric: States the regular client does not mine or earn coins
Mentions early versions had a built-in miner that was removed
Explains CPU mining is now negligible versus network hashpower
Lists ways to obtain bitcoin today (dedicated mining hardware, selling goods, exchanges)
Penalize: suggesting running a full node pays block rewards

in_pack_facts.fact: Client stores keys, does not mine
in_pack_facts.quote: The standard client does not mine coins, it stores the keys you use to access them.
The earlier versions of the client did include a "miner" which generated bitcoins.

source.title: Does the Bitcoin client generate bitcoins automatically?

question: What do people mean by calling themselves bitcoin maximalists, and why do they hold that view?
rubric: Defines maximalism as seeing bitcoin as the only cryptocurrency worth holding or building on
Mentions the decentralisation argument (unknown creator, no central authority)
Mentions fair distribution (no pre-mine or pre-sale)
Mentions the most proof-of-work / most secure argument or that improvements can be added to bitcoin
Penalize: presenting maximalism as an official organisation

in_pack_facts.quote: There was no pre-sale for insiders, no pre-mine, everyone had the opportunity to mine right from the start.
Bitcoin has the most proof of work going into it, making it the "most secure" chain.

source.title: What does bitcoin maximalist mean?

question: A few of my LND channels have nearly all the liquidity on the far side. How can I even them out while keeping them open?
rubric: States LND has no native rebalance command
Names an external tool such as lndmanage or rebalance-lnd
Explains rebalancing is a circular payment that costs routing fees
Mentions the target of roughly 50-50 balance or questioning the need
Penalize: recommending closing and reopening channels as the only option

in_pack_facts.quote: Such rebalancing will cost you routing fees as they are regular (circular) payments.
resulting in a 50-50 balance on the channel you specified

source.title: How to manually rebalance Lightning Network channels?

question: Roughly how much disk space did the full Bitcoin block chain need in mid-2012?
rubric: Gives approximately 2.6 GB as the mid-2012 size
Mentions continued growth (e.g. around 11 MB a day or block count ~187,600)
Mentions lightweight clients/e-wallets as alternatives for low disk space
Notes the different trust/security model of those alternatives
Penalize: giving present-day sizes of hundreds of gigabytes for 2012

in_pack_facts.quote: At the moment, it's about 2.6GB, but it will be growing with time.
You can try looking into using an eWallet or some lightweight clients if you are tight on the disc space.

source.title: How big is the blockchain on disk as of 5th July 2012?

question: I'd like to check my Ledger balance without plugging the device in. Can the extended public key do that?
rubric: Confirms an xpub allows watch-only balance monitoring
Names a tool such as a block explorer, Sentinel or Electrum
Notes tools only scan a limited range of addresses (gap) and may miss some
Notes the xpub cannot spend funds
Penalize: telling the user to export the private key or seed to check balances

in_pack_facts.quote: only search a few addresses (all of the ones that have been used in a transaction and then some number ahead of those) so it may miss some of your transactions
That's exactly what the Sentinel app does: imports a read-only XPUB key in order to passively watch the balance of an offline wallet

source.title: Is it possible to use xpub address to monitor balance from previously generated addresses?

question: What usually explains those days when Bitcoin transactions paid absurdly large fees?
rubric: States most spikes are user or software errors
Explains forgotten change outputs become fees
Mentions unit/decimal errors (satoshi conversion)
Mentions the network accepts underspending inputs, so errors go to miners
Penalize: claiming large fees are mandatory or set by the protocol

in_pack_facts.quote: raw transactions are incredibly easy to screw up since you must explicitly pay yourself if you want change
will happily accept transactions if you're spending much less than the inputs

source.title: Are the huge transaction fees mostly mistakes or some other market indicator?

Explains halving every 210,000 blocks (about four years)
Mentions the subsidy eventually falls below one satoshi (block 6,930,000)
Mentions 99% issued by around 2036
Penalize: claiming all 21 million will be mined by 2040

in_pack_facts.quote: therefore the last block creating new bitcoins will be block 6,929,999
In 2036 99% of the bitcoins will be in circulation, in 2048 it will be 99.9%.

question: I'm reproducing the attack that pulls a private key from two ECDSA signatures sharing a nonce, but my result is wrong. What could I be missing?
rubric: Explains the s versus -s (mod N) malleability
Lists the four candidate formulas for k
Says to keep the candidate where k*G has x equal to r
Gives the private key formula (s*k - z)/r and checks it against the public key
Penalize: claiming nonce reuse cannot leak the private key

in_pack_facts.quote: you can always replace `s` with `-s` (mod N) and the signature is still valid
you have to make a list of candidates for `k` (kandidates?) and then select whichever one actually works

source.title: Recovering private key when someone uses the same k twice in ECDSA signatures

question: Explain how a lightweight SPV wallet verifies payments compared with a full node.

States SPV downloads only block headers rather than the full chain
States full nodes verify every transaction against consensus rules
Mentions SPV trusts proof-of-work difficulty or connected nodes

MultiBit, Bitcoin Wallet for Android, and Electrum are examples of SPV clients.

question: Why can't a bitcoin public key be recovered from the address it belongs to?
rubric: States the address is a hash (SHA-256 and RIPEMD-160) of the public key
Explains hashes are one-way functions
Mentions the size difference (160-bit address vs ~257-bit key)
Says the public key becomes visible when the address first spends
Penalize: claiming the address is the public key itself

in_pack_facts.quote: The address is only 160-bits. The public key is 257-bits.
From that point on, the public key corresponding to the address is publicly known.

source.title: Why is it impossible to derive public key from address?

question: Tell me what an ASIC miner is and why it beats a regular computer at mining.
rubric: Expands ASIC as application-specific integrated circuit
Explains it is designed for a single task (Bitcoin hashing)
Contrasts with flexible but inefficient general-purpose CPUs
Mentions large speed gains (e.g. GH/s, >1,000 times a PC) and high power draw
Penalize: describing an ASIC as software or a mining pool

in_pack_facts.quote: Because Bitcoin miners only ever use their chips for Bitcoin mining, you can make chips that are really really fast
which is over 1,200 times faster than the average computer

source.title: What does "ASIC" mean?

question: Tell me whether a majority-hashrate attack rewriting history could be noticed and what honest users could do.
rubric: States the attack is detectable as a large chain reorganization
Mentions the REORGANIZE entry in debug.log
Explains invalidated transactions can be resubmitted unless double-spent
Mentions the risk that rejecting deep reorgs can permanently split the network

in_pack_facts.quote: you'll see a `REORGANIZE` in the client's `debug.log` file
the network can permanently split with each side rejecting the other side's block chain as a suspicious reorganization

question: Several websites promise me free bitcoin if I give them my address. Are these faucets legit, and is sharing my address dangerous?

today most faucets only give out minuscule amounts of bitcoin, usually not worth your time and effort
